title: Carlsberg India Pvt. Ltd vs Panchmukhi Enterprises on 22 September, 2023
full_text: Carlsberg India Pvt. Ltd vs Panchmukhi Enterprises on 22 September, 2023 DLND020146302017 IN THE COURT OF METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE-04, NEW DELHI DISTRICT, PATIALA HOUSE COURTS, NEW DELHI - PRESIDED BY: PARAS DALAL, D.J.S. CT. CASES No. 17164/ 2017 M/s. CARLSBERG INDIA PVT. LTD. v. PANCHMUKHI ENTERPRISES & OTHERS P.S. BARAKHAMBA ROAD Ct. Cases No. 17164/2017 CNR No. DLND02-014630-2017 Date of Institution 09.06.2017 Name, parentage and address of complainant M/s. Carlsberg India Pvt. Ltd. Office at: 4th Floor, Rectangle no.1, Commercial Complex, D4, Saket New Delhi-110017 Name, parentage and address of the accused no.1 Panchmukhi Enterprises Office at: Shop No. 45, 46, Old Rajinder Nagar Market, New Delhi Name, parentage and address of the accused no.2 Mr. Ajay Tyagi (Sole-proprietor of Panchmukhi Enterprises) R/o: Plot no. 3, Khasra No.26/3, 4, 7, 8, Nangli Sakrawati Industrial Area, New Delhi - 110043 Offence complained off 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 Plea of Accused Not Guilty Final Order Conviction Date of Judgment 22.09.2023 Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 1 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Argued by: Sh. Manu Prabhakar, Ld. Counsel for the complainant company. Sh. Vishal Bhatnagar, Ms. Lata Walia and Sh. Anand Prakash, Ld. Counsels for the accused no.2. JUDGMENT BRIEF STATEMENT OF THE REASONS FOR DECISION : - 1. Vide this judgment, this Court shall dispose off complaint for offence punishable under Section 138 of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 filed by the complainant company. In gist, it is alleged that complainant was in business dealing with the accused no.1 being sole proprietorship firm of accused no.2 in supply of material/ goods i.e. beer to the accused, regular invoices were raised and payments were received from the accused no.2 in lump sum. Complainant alleged that as per books of accounts regularly maintained by complainant, after adjusting the part payments received from the accused persons, a sum of Rs.19,85,228 was outstanding. In discharge of his liability qua the repayment of outstanding amount, complainant alleged that accused drew cheque in question Ex.CW1/F of Rs.19,85,228/-. Complainant presented the cheque, but same was dishonored vide memo Ex.CW1/G with reason 'Funds insufficient'. The complainant sent a legal demand notice on 21.04.2017 Ex.CW1/H through courier vide receipts Ex.CW1/I to Ex.CW1/M which were returned or delivered vide report Ex.CW1/N to Ex.CW1/L, however, accused did not make payment within statutory period of legal demand notice, hence, this complaint. PRE-SUMMONING EVIDENCE & NOTICE 2. Pre-summoning evidence was lead by the complainant side and after hearing complainant side, accused was summoned for offence punishable under Section 138 of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. After appearance of accused, it was ensured that copy of complaint has been supplied. Notice was put to the accused by my scholarly predecessor for offence punishable under Section 138 of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 on 16.03.2021 Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 2 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises to which accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. It was stated by accused that the cheque was given as security to the complainant and same was blank signed cheque. Accused further stated that he did not fill the details of the cheque and complainant had misused the same. The accused admitted the address of Old Rajinder Nagar where the notice was sent, however he stated that the Najafgarh address was incorrect. The accused was granted opportunity to cross examine the complainant witnesses. COMPLAINANT EVIDENCE 3. Complainant in his pre-summoning evidence examined its then Authorised Representative (hereinafter referred to as 'AR') Mr. Harshdeep Khanna, however before complainant evidence stage, he left the services and hence complainant company sought to substitute its new AR Mr. Vishal Nassa, which was allowed by the Court vide Order dated 18.10.2019. Then AR Mr. Vishal Nassa deposed by way of affidavit dated 24.01.2019 which was tendered before the Court on 06.06.2022 relying on the averment in the affidavit identical to the complaint as well as all the documents placed on record from Ex.CW1/C1 to Ex.CW1/V. 4. AR of the Complainant company was subjected to cross examination and he answered that he joined the organisation in the year 2016, but admitted to have not filed appointment letter. He stated that he knew the contents of affidavit dated 24.01.2019 which was attested in Patiala House Court on 10.03.2019 and admitted the signatures on the affidavit to be his. CW1 about the transaction deposed that he knew the accused and business transaction took place in his presence as accused had visited his office personally. CW1 stated that he knew the formalities undertaken by the complainant company during providing credit facilities. He stated that security cheques are not taken during the providing of credit facilities, however he admitted to have filed no copy of procedures/ formalities being followed by the Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 3 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises complainant company. CW1 after being shown the original cheque Ex.CW1/F answered that cheque was not signed in his presence, although he stated that the signatures to be of the accused. CW1 then voluntarily stated that he had seen other cheques signed by the accused and they bore the same signatures. CW1 further stated that he had not filed earlier cheques, as payments were already cleared qua them. CW1 pleaded ignorance as to who filled the other particulars of the cheque in question and voluntarily stated that cheques are collected by their sales department. CW1 then stated that accused was dealing with the complainant company even prior to his joining. Attention of witness was then drawn to invoices Ex.CW1/C (colly) and he answered that he was not aware of the exact amounts of the invoices, but then voluntarily stated that as the payment comes in round of lumpsum amount and not as per invoices. CW1 further stated that invoices alongwith the complaint are of the lumpsum amount due and admitted that total amount raised in the invoices do not match with the cheque amount. CW1 then after seeing the legal notice Ex.CW1/H admitted that it did not bear his signatures and again after seeing Ex.CW1/D stated that same is ledger filed by the company. CW1 then stated that he was aware of the amount paid by the accused after 2016, however could not tell the exact amount. CW1 further stated that he was aware than accused made payment of Rs.6,00,000/- after receiving the legal notice Ex.CW1/H and admitted that same was not mentioned in the ledger Ex.CW1/D, however he voluntarily clarified that ledger was prepared before payment of Rs.6,00,000/- was made. CW1 was then drawn to paragraph no.16 of his affidavit and was asked to show document where rate of interest @ 24% is to be adjusted in case of delaying payment and CW1 could not show any such document. CW1 was then questioned about written agreement between both the sides to which he answered that no such agreement was executed and it was not required since customer used excise permit to do business with the complainant company. CW1 then answered that payment was made on oral mutual agreement between the parties and no internal procedure of the company exists regarding the modes, procedures and methods of payment also the business transaction. CW1 Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 4 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises then voluntarily stated that no cash was accepted and only mode of payment allowed was RTGS and cheque. CW1 then deposed that invoices Ex.CW1/C (Colly) were given by the company to the accused and they were sent alongwith consignment to the customer. CW1 admitted that invoices Ex.CW1/C did not bear signatures of accused. CW1 also admitted that except legal notice no information was given to the accused regarding outstanding amount shown in the invoices, however voluntarily stated that communication happened through sales department and they updated the accused about the outstanding dues. CW1 however admitted that he had filed no such document showing the information sent to the accused regarding the outstanding amount by the sales department, however he denied the suggestion that accused had no existing enforceable liability at the time of issuance of cheque and further denied that complainant company misused the cheque in question of the accused. Complainant company did not examine any other witnesses in the complainant evidence stage and accordingly complainant evidence was closed vide statement of AR on 06.06.2022. STATEMENT OF ACCUSED 5. The statement of accused was recorded under Section 313 of The Code of Criminal Procedure , 1973 read with Section 281 of The Code of Criminal Procedure , 1973 separately on 27.09.2022. Incriminating evidence was put to him. Accused answered that he had issued cheque in question in favour of the complainant as security and had signed the same, however rest of the particulars were not filled by him. Accused further defended that since cheque was issued as security and no information was given prior to its presentation, same was dishonoured for reason 'funds insufficient'. Accused also denied receiving legal demand notice and when given opportunity to further defend stated that he used to take material from the complainant company and it insisted on security cheque and hence present cheque in question duly signed was given as security for future transaction. Accused defended that he had already made payment and had no liability towards the complainant company and Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 5 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises cheque was issued in 2015. Accused also stated that complainant company stopped their business in Delhi after the year 2015 and they misused the cheque in question. DEFENCE EVIDENCE 6. Accused chose to lead defence evidence and moved application under Section 315 CrPC, which was allowed. On 16.05.2023, accused as DW1 deposed that he started business with the complainant company in the year 2014-15 and received invoices from 2014- 15 itself from the complainant company. DW1 stated that procedure to start the business with complainant company was to have the copy of license, security cheque, copy of aadhar card and pan card and he was also made to submit 3-4 cheques in the year 2014-15 with the complainant company. DW1 stated that the disputed cheque no. 262955 Ex.CW1/F was also part and parcel of submission of 3-4 security cheque with the complainant. DW1 stated that there was no liability at the time when disputed cheque was submitted with the complainant company as there was no business started in the year 2014-15. He further stated that the statement of account Ex.CW1/D was never handed over to him and claim of complainant company in Ex.CW1/D, the posting date i.e. 11.03.2016 is wrong as business with the complainant company was started in the year 2014-15. DW1 further stated that he made payments to the complainant in year 2014-15 itself and had done the business with the complainant company from 2014-15 to 2016-17, but he did not remember how much payment was made. DW1 further stated that he made payment to complainant company till 2016-17 and relied on the ledger filed by the complainant company to support the same. DW1 further stated that complainant company wound up its business till the year 2017 and did not do business til 2020. DW1 then stated that complainant company handed over complete business to one Mohan Gold Water and he had done business with the said company and same was only different name, however belonged to the complainant company since they changed their name to Mohan Gold Water only for business in Delhi jurisdiction. DW1 also stated that he Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 6 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises was doing business with Mohan Gold Water till 2020 and they did not seek any payment nor made any correspondence with regard to due payment. DW1 stated that Mohan Gold Water put a pre-condition to do business i.e. to make payment to complainant company and this showed that complainant company owned Mohan Gold Water and DW1 further stated to have made payment to complainant company through RTGS till 2020, however he again could not tell the exact payment made. DW1 then deposed that as per the carton, the incentive scheme which was decided with the complainant company was not given to him and incentive which was given was around 40 Rupees per carton, whereas the commitment given by the complainant company was 160 Rupees per carton. DW1 also stated that in the year 2016, when complainant company did not renew its license, at that point of time, he was proposed by the complainant company to have one + one which means he would get one bottle free with one bottle, however DW1 alleged that same was not given and in the year 2019, the complainant company proposed to make a payment of Rs.1,00,000/- outstanding as there was no outstanding with regard to the complainant company. DW1 then reiterated that cheque in question Ex.CW1/F was only signed by him and nothing had been filed by him in the cheque. DW1 was then cross examined by the counsel for the complainant and he answered that no receiving of security cheque was given by the complainant company to him. DW1 further stated that he never prepared any statement of account at his end for the transaction which used to happen with the complainant company. DW1 further stated that he brought no document on record stating his business relation with company namely, Mohan Gold Water, however he voluntarily stated that he can given details of payment made to The Mohan Gold Water as he had done business with the said company and that is the reason the payment has been made to the said company. DW1 admitted to have no proof given by the complainant company pertaining to incentive of 160 Rs. Per carton and one bottle free with bottle, however he voluntarily stated that Hon'ble Supreme Court's Rule had made a rule that no offer of any such kind can be given. Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 7 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises 7. Accused closed his defence evidence on 12.07.2023. Final arguments from complainant side heard on 25.08.2023. Case file perused. POINTS FOR DETERMINATION : - 8. Whether the complainant has been able to establish ingredients of offence punishable under Section 138 of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 beyond shadow of reasonable doubt against the accused or not? 9. Final order. APPRECIATION OF FACTS/CONTENTIONS/ANALYSIS & FINDINGS 10. To bring home conviction for offence punishable under Section 138 of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the complainant is obliged to prove : - (a) The cheque(s) was/were drawn/issued by the accused person(s) to the complainant on an account maintained by him/her/them/it with the bank for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or liability. (b) The cheques(s) was/were presented to the bank within a period of six months or within period of its/their validity. (c) The cheque(s) so presented for encashment was/were dishonored. (d) The payee/complainant of the cheque(s) issued a Legal Demand Notice within 30 days from the receipt of information from the bank regarding dishonourment of the cheque(s). (e) The drawer of the cheque(s) failed to make the payment within 15 days of receipt of afore-said Legal Demand Notice. (f) The complaint was presented within 30 days after the expiry of above 15 days. Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 8 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises UNDISPUTED/UNCONTROVERTED FACTS 11. At the outset, it is pertinent to mention herein that it is not in dispute that cheque in question belong to the accused, it bears his signatures, it was drawn on an account maintained by the accused with a bank, cheque in question was dishonored as alleged, legal demand notice was sent to correct Old Rajinder Nagar address of accused and accused failed to make the payment of cheque in question till date. So, there is no need of discussion qua said ingredients and same can be regarded as being duly proved on record and being non- controverted. CONTENTIONS QUA NON ADHERENCE TO TIME SCHEDULE 12. The first contention of the defense is that complainant has failed to adhere to time schedule stipulated in Section 138 and 142 NI Act and hence complaint is not maintainable and even barred by limitation. 13. It is necessary to lay down the time lines of each event in the present case. Complainant side has relied on cheque, return memo, demand notice and date of filing which is not disputed by the accused side. Be that as it may, the contention as to actual date of information of dishour, actual due delivery of demand notice are not considered (same shall be discussed in the further part of this judgment) and dates mentioned in the documents are presumed to be true. The cheque is dated 22.03.2017 (thus having validity till 22.06.2017). Same was presented and returned dishonoured on 24.03.2017 (thus demand notice was to be sent by 24.04.2017 since date of reckoning is to be excluded). The demand notice is dated 21.04.2017 and courier receipts are dated 22.04.2017 and 24.04.2017. The complainant side relies on delivery dates of 25.04.2017, 27.04.2017 and 28.04.2017. Even if first delivery of 25.04.2017 is taken into consideration, the accused had to make payment on or before Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 9 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises 10.05.2017 and accordingly cause of action arose in favour of complainant company on 11.05.2017 (last date of filing thus was 11.06.2017). The complainant company filed the present complaint on 07.06.2017 and cognizance was taken by this Court on 09.06.2017. 14. Based on the above time lines of the present case, this Court finds no fault in maintainability of present complaint as per period prescribed by the Act, 1881. CONTENTIONS QUA LEGAL DEMAND NOTICE 15. The next major contention which has been raised by accused in this matter is that accused has not received any legal demand notice, therefore, ingredients of offence punishable under Section 138 of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 are not complete, hence accused should be acquitted in this matter. Defence has even relied on one judgment passed by the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka M. Nagappa v. Mohamad Aslam Savanur; 31.03.2021. 16. Per contra, it is contention of the complainant side that the legal demand notice was sent through a registered and reputed courier service to the accused on his correct address as admitted of Old Rajinder Nagar, New Delhi and as per tracking report same was delivered, therefore, accused should be held guilty in this matter. 17. Submissions of both sides considered. This Court sees no substance in this defence of accused side. It is not the case of accused side that legal demand notice was not sent vide courier receipt and tracking report available on record on his correct address of Old Rajinder Nagar. The accused in notice of accusation under Section 251 CrPC himself admitted that the address of Old Rajinder Nagar was correct. The fact that accused Ajay Tyagi is sole-proprietor of Panchmukhi Enterprises is not under dispute and further that Panchmukhi Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 10 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises Enterprises has its address at Old Rajinder Nagar. It is trite law that sole-proprietorship has no separate legal entity and sole-proprietor and sole-proprietorship is one and same. Even a letter to any of the two is valid service. In this backdrop attention is drawn to notice of demand dated 21.04.2017 Ex.CW1/H and particularly serial no. 1 wherein Panchmukhi Enterprises through Proprietor (Ajay Tyagi) was issued notice at Shop No. 45, 46, Old Rajinder Nagar Market, New Delhi-60. Also courier receipt Ex.CW1/M issued by DTDC bearing no. V37039184. Against the said receipt the tracking report on record is Ex.CW1/U wherein the item has been successfully delivered on 25.04.2023. This Court can thus conclusively hold that demand notice Ex.CW1/H was successfully delivered to the accused vide receipt Ex.CW1/M and report is Ex.CW1/U. Defence may be correct that since it is private courier service, no help can be drawn from Section 27 General Clauses Act, 1899. However, the defense fails to take note of Section 114 Evidence Act. This Court is within its power to draw a presumption of existence of factum of delivery of notice through private courier which had common course of private business, in the facts of the present case. Section 138 does not prescribe the mode of sending of demand notice, same can be post, courier and even be delivered on text message, email or social media platform. 18. Once, it is not disputed and proved on record that the legal demand notice was sent to correct address of the accused then the defence of the accused side that accused side has not received any legal demand notice is no defence in the eyes of law in view of the judgment passed by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in matter of " C. C. Alavi Hazi Vs. Palapetty Mohd. & Anr. " reported in (2007) 6 Supreme Court Cases 555. In said judgment, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has held that : - "Any drawer who claims that he did not received the notice sent by post, can, within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court in respect of complaint Under Section 138 of the Act, make the payment of the cheque amount and submit to the court that he had made the payment within 15 days of the receipt of summons (by receiving a copy of complaint with the summons) and, therefore, the Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 11 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises complainant is liable to be rejected. A person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court along-with the copy of complaint Under Section 138 of the Act, can not obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as required Under Section 138 , by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary Under Section 27 of G. C. Act and 114 of the Evidence Act ." In this case, since, the accused side has not made payment of cheque(s) amount in question within 15 days of the receipt of summons of this Court, therefore, in the light of above-said judgment and discussions, this Court is of the opinion that defence of the accused side that he has not received any legal demand notice is without any force and is hereby rejected. 19. This Court also fails to understand the reliance by the defence on the M. Nagappa case (Supra). In the given case the trial court finding that there was no proper service of posting by private courier was set-aside and infact the acquittal on this ground was reversed and accused was convicted. In relying the said judgment, the defence has helped the complainant in showing that it is the accused who has to show by placing cogent and convincing evidence that demand notice was intentionally sent on wrong address. The said reliance on the judgment is to the advantage of the complainant that a demand notice under Section 138 NI Act, need not be through India post only. The provisions requires demand notice, but the manner is not prescribed. Thus even a registered courier can be a valid mode to serve the demand notice. CONTENTIONS QUA CONSIDERATION 20. The contentions against non-existence of consideration as raised by the defence is two fold - 1. that complainant failed to acknowledge payment of Rs.6,00,000/- made by the accused after the cheque was dishonoured and complainant further improved on his complaint at the post-summoning evidence stage, even though it was admitted that payment of Rs.6,00,000 was made by the accused to the complainant before filing of the present case; and Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 12 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises 2. there was no outstanding liability qua the cheque which was given as blank signed security cheque and the invoices as well as account statement relied by the complainant are not proved in accordance with law. Apart from these two fold defence, the accused in his deposition also stated that complainant was still in business with him till 2020 under changed name of Mohan Gold Water and also that incentive as per commitment was never adjusted by the complainant. Further, it was argued that complainant's AR himself admitted that the amount of cheque and total of invoices do not match and there was no express communication that interest @24% per annum was to be charged in delayed payment. 21. On the other hand, it is the contention of the complainant side that it is not denied that both sides were in business terms and did business till 2016. Complainant side argued that accused has not denied cheque belongs to him and he signed the same. Complainant side further argued that even one of the address to which the demand notice was sent was admitted to be correct and despite service of notice the accused made no payment. However, in admission of his liability, he made a payment of Rs.6,00,000 to the complainant company, hence, all ingredients of commission of offence punishable under Section 138 of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 stands established on record, therefore, accused should be held guilty in this matter. 22. Submissions of both side considered. The provisions which are involved are - Section 118 (a) of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 provides as under : - " Section 118 . Presumption as to negotiable instruments.- Until the contrary is proved, the following presumption shall be made:- (a) of consideration- that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, was indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration;........." 23. Section 139 of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 provides as under :- Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 13 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises " Section 139 Presumption in favour of holder.- It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability." 24. In matter of " Krishna Janardhan Bhat Vs. Dattatraya G. Hegde " (2008) 4 SCC 54, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has observed : - "32. An accused for discharging the burden of proof placed upon him under a statute need not examine himself. He may discharge his burden on the basis of the materials already brought on record. An accused has a constitutional right to maintain silence. Standard of proof on the part of the accused and that of the prosecution in a criminal case is different." "34. Furthermore, whereas prosecution must prove the guilty of an accused beyond all reasonable doubt, the standard of proof so as to prove a defence on the part of the accused is 'preponderance of probabilities'. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies." 25. In matter of " Mallavarapu Kasivisweswara Rao Vs. Thadikonda Ramulu Firm " (2008) 7 SCC 655, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India (though it was a civil matter related to promissory note, but is relevant to refer herein) has held : - "17. Under Section 118 (a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the court is obliged to presume, until the contrary is proved, that the promissory note was made for consideration. It is also a settled position that the initial burden in this regard lies on the defendant to prove the non-existence of consideration by brining on record such facts and circumstances which would lead the court to believe the non-existence of the consideration either by direct evidence or by preponderance of probabilities showing that the existence of consideration was improbable, doubtful or illegal." 26. In matter of " Bharat Barrel & Drum Mfg. Co. V. Amin Chand Payrelal " (1999) 3 SCC 35, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India (though it was also a civil matter related to promissory note, but is relevant to refer herein) has held : - "12. Upon consideration of various judgments as noted hereinabove, the position of law which emerges is that once execution of the promissory note is admitted, the presumption under Section 118 (a) would arise that it is supported by a consideration. Such a presumption is rebuttable. The defendant can prove the non-existence of a consideration by raising a probable defence. If the defendant Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 14 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises is proved to have discharged the initial onus of proof showing that the existence of consideration was improbable or doubtful or the same was illegal, the onus would shift to the plaintiff who will be obliged to prove it as a matter of fact and upon its failure to prove would disentitle him to the grant of relief on the basis of the negotiable instrument. The burden upon the defendant of proving the non-existence of the consideration can be either direct or by bringing on record the preponderance of probabilities by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies. In such an event, the plaintiff is entitled under the law to rely upon all the evidence led in the case including that of the plaintiff as well. In case, where the defendant fails to discharge the initial onus of proof by showing the non-existence of the consideration, the plaintiff would invariably be held entitled to the benefit of presumption arising under Section 118 (a) in his favour. The court may not insist upon the defendant to disprove the existence of consideration by leading direct evidence as the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated and even if led, is to be seen with a doubt. The bare denial of the passing of the consideration apparently does not appear to be any defence. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the benefit of shifting the onus of proving to the plaintiff. To disprove the presumption, the defendant has to bring on record such facts and circumstances upon consideration of which the court may either believe that the consideration did not exist or its non-existence was so probable that a prudent man would, under the circumstances of the case, shall act upon the plea that it did not exist." 27. In matter of " Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan " (2010) 11 SCC 441 which is a Full Bench Decision, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India while discussing above said provisions, judgments and other case law on the point has held : - "26. In light of these extracts, we are in agreement with the respondent claimant that the presumption mandated by Section 139 of the Act does indeed include the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. To the extent, the impugned observations in Krishna Janardhan Bhat may not be correct. However, this does not in any way cast doubt on the correctness of the decision in that case since it was based on the specific facts and circumstances therein. As noted in the citations, this is of course in the nature of a rebuttable presumption and it is open to the accused to raise a defence wherein the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability can be contested. However, there can be no doubt that there is an initial presumption which favours the complainant". "27. Section 139 of the Act is an example of a reverse onus clause that has been included in furtherance of the legislative objective of improving the credibility of negotiable instruments. While Section 138 of the Act specifies a strong criminal remedy in relation to the dishonour of cheques, the rebuttable presumption under Section 139 is a device to prevent undue delay in the course of litigation. However, it must be remembered that the offence made punishable by Section 138 can be better described as a regulatory offence since the bouncing of a cheque is largely in the nature of a civil wrong whose impact is usually confined to the private parties involved in commercial transactions. In such a scenario, the test Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 15 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises of proportionality should guide the construction and interpretation of reverse onus clauses and the defendant-accused cannot be expected to discharge an unduly high standard or proof." "28. In the absence of compelling justifications, reverse onus clauses usually impose an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. Keeping this in view, it is a settled position that when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubt about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. As clarified in the citations, the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own." 28. So, precisely there is initial presumption of legally enforceable debt or liability against the accused side, but same is rebuttable. The standard of proof for rebuttal is preponderance of probabilities. Accused side can lead evidence in defence, even can rely on materials submitted by complainant and can rely upon circumstances also to show non- existence of consideration or it being improbable and need not adduce evidence of his own for the same. 29. Before discussing the merits of this case, it is necessary to settle the admitted fact between parties with regard to business relations. Complainant used to supply material/goods i.e. beer to the accused and same was not vide any written agreement. Complainant made no averments of their business terms, however, accused as DW1 deposed that he produced some of his documents and particularly his liquor license and thus complainant supplied to him the material. The supply vide invoices is also admitted and accused denied maintaining any account statement of good received, returned or payments made. The accused however in his examination in chief as DW1 categorically referred to the proof of payment done by him through the account statement filed on record by the complainant company. These fact in the present case are not denied by either side. The Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 16 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises invoices itself records that late payments would attract penalty of interest of Rs.24% per annum. 30. Now, the defence of the accused side to be considered first is about non- disclosure of Rs.6,00,000/- received by the complainant company before the case was filed. The complainant side during trial and even at the time of final argument has admitted receipt of Rs.6,00,000/- between 31.05.2017 to 31.07.2019. Complainant side even admits that said Rs.6,00,000 was qua the cheque in question. Complainant side during deposition as CW1 and argument even clarified that on the date of the cheque the amount due was Rs.19,85,225 where as the invoices on record was of total Rs.19,99,200/-. Thus on the date of the cheque the amount due was more than amount stated in the cheque and admittedly the payments were made after issuance of demand notice. In said eventuality, the defense that complainant ought to have adhered to Section 56 NI Act is not maintainable. When on the date of the cheque, the amount due was allegedly more than the cheque amount, the complainant company was correct in presenting the same for payment. Further, even on the date of sending of the demand notice, the same amount was due. The only question which requires deliberation is why the complaint filed before the Court on 07.06.2017 failed to mention one Rs.50,000/- received on 30.05.2017. 31. The complainant company came with a simplest of answers that once payment was not received qua the outstanding liability, the matter was referred by the company to its legal department. The legal department got the demand notice issued and as per delivery on 25.04.2017, no payment was received within 15 days i.e. 10.05.2017. Thereafter, the complainant company's legal department initiated filing of the present case. The complainant company further stated that payment of Rs.50,000/- only was not within 15 days of receipt of Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 17 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises demand notice or qua the entire claim of the cheque and thus the same was not brought to the notice of legal department between 30.05.2017 to 07.06.2017. 32. On the very face the explanation of the complainant company is natural and seems probable. Complainant company i.e. Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. supplying liquor and other material obviously would have different departments and presumably finance and legal department would be separate. Besides, the accused seeks rejection of entire claim of complainant by mere payment of Rs.50,000/- against cheque in question amount of Rs.19,85,225/-. The said payment of Rs.50,000/- admittedly on 30.05.2017 is not within 15 days window as per Section 138 NI Act which was open till only 10.05.2017. Since no payment was made within 15 days, the cause of action arose in favour of the complainant company qua the cheque in question. Accused could have escaped criminal consequences by paying the amount of the cheque and not just small portion of the claim. If such a defense is accepted, any drawer would escape liability under Section 138 NI Act by paying a mere portion of amount of the cheque. The defence cannot be allowed to take advantage of one provisions of the law when it himself has not adhered to the other provisions. The complainant company thus had already cause of action in its favour on 16 th day of receipt of demand notice i.e. 11.05.2017. 33. True that complainant company could have accepted receipt of Rs.50,000/- on 30.05.2017 in its complaint filed on 07.06.2017. However, as already held that complainant company already had cause of action in its favour and it is quite possible that its legal department was seized of the matter and financial department had not informed about receipt of Rs.50,000/- between 30.05.2017 to 07.06.2017. Based on the cause of action, even the notice of accusation was framed and accused made no specific defence of making exact payment. The complainant however was genuine to accept the receipt of Rs.50,000/- on Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 18 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises 30.05.2017 and other Rs.5,50,000/- until 31.07.2019. The AR of the complainant company in post-summoning evidence stated receipt of these monies and even in his cross examination accepted and clarified all the above facts. 34. This Court thus finds no tenable ground to the accused side that present complaint is not maintainable under Section 138 r/w 142 NI Act for not accepting receipt of monies in the complainant made after the cause of action arose in favour of the complainant. 35. The next defence of the accused side is that the very first ingredient of Section 138 is not made out since there was no legally recoverable debt. The defence seeks support from the complainant's AR's testimony who admitted that the invoices does not carry receiving from the accused, the total of invoices did not match the amount stated in the cheque and also that the ledger account statement does not have signatures of accused. The defence thus argued that there is no proof that the material as per invoices were delivered and account statement filed by complainant was true or acknowledged by the accused and hence any claim against the said amount is not legally recoverable debt. The defence has been vehement in arguing that Section 138 NI Act postulates legally recoverable debt, however what and how much is the legally recoverable debt is always a question which complainant has to prove. The defence finally argued that complainant took blank cheque as security and without any correspondence with the accused, filled the same and presented it before the Bank and is now claiming the amount and same cannot be a legally recoverable debt merely by unilateral action of the complainant. The complainant side on the other hand take recourse to Section 118 NI Act and plead that a presumption already exists in their favour and since cheque was drawn of the amount, the accused is now duty bound to discharge his burden of proof that no such amount of the cheque was due. Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 19 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises 36. At first the contention qua security cheque needs determination. It is settled law that even qua a security cheque, complaint is maintainable provided the complainant can show that there was outstanding liability of the drawer towards the payee/ complainant as on the date of the cheque. Further, Section 49 of the NI Act allows an instrument indorsed in blank to be converted into indorsement in full. There is a specific provision which allows a holder of an instrument to indorse the negotiable instrument 'in full' and the only requirement is that there ought to be a valid consideration/ legally recoverable debt. Same preposition has been upheld in catena of judgment. The two defence of the accused that cheque was for security and was only signed in blank holds no ground, even if assumed to be true. The only consideration before this Court now is whether on the date of the cheque there was outstanding liability on the accused to the amount of the cheque in question. 37. Qua the above issue, the complainant lays reliance on testimonies of CW1 and DW1 to show the manner in which business between them was transacted. Further, complainant relies on invoices,, as well as account statement Ex.CW1/D. Section 34 Evidence Act provides relevancy to such books of accounts maintained in regular course of business. The provision although clarifies that such statement are not by itself sufficient evidence to charge a person of liability but the present case squarely falls within the provisions of the section. The statement of account Ex.CW1/D is relevant as per the provision and since the same itself is not sufficient to charge accused with liability, however the liability falls from the cheque in question which seeks support from the account statement. The invoices/ bills and account statement thus being relevant are to be proved by the complainant. 38. The accused side raised a valid objection as to proving of the account statement and invoices which does not bear the signatures of the accused. CW1 even admitted neither the invoices/ bills nor the account statement bears accused's signature. However, there is an Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 20 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises implied admission in the present case by the accused. Accused in his evidence DW1 deposed about the manner in which business was transacted between the parties. Accused admits that material was supplied by the complainant and he used to make payment in lump sum and never qua any particular invoice/ bill. There was no written agreement or any account statement exchanged between parties regularly, everything was by word of mouth and arranged orally agreed. DW1 also specifically laid reliance on the statement of accounts Ex.CW1/D filed by the complainant to show that he used to make payments. The accused was then specifically asked to show any invoices, account statement, ledger or book of account of kept by him qua the transactions with the complainant, however he specifically deposed that he kept no such record and he used to make payment as raised by the complainant and his payments were even reflected in the account statement maintained by the complainant. The said admission on part of the accused is sufficient to prove the Ex.CW1/D and further in the Evidence Act under Section 58 , a fact admitted need not require proof. This Court does not believe the accused that its firm did not make any record, statement of accounts, ledger or even proof of sales record. The excise department of the Government mandates records of each sale of the liquor including beer. This statement of the accused is incriminating on his part that he never used to maintain any record and alteast the accused could have proved his sale of beer supplied by the complainant and payment made to show that all material supplied were paid. It seems that accused is yet to make a payment and even his accounts shows outstanding liability, he has not placed on record any document. Section 106 Evidence Act casts a specific duty on the party to prove any fact within its knowledge. Payments and accounts maintained by the accused would be within his knowledge and he ought to have proved the same as per provisions of the law. 39. Based on the above discussion, the account statement Ex.CW1/D stands proved. The cheque admittedly bears the signature of the accused and particulars even if filled Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 21 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises by the complainant is permitted under the NI Act . The parties are in agreement that amount of the invoices are more than the amount in the cheque and complainant has presented the same to its bank. After dishonourment, demand notice was issued and accused failed to make payment within 15 days. Cause of action arose and present complaint was filed. 40. Before returning the findings, some of the defence ought to be discussed. The defence that complainant failed to account for payments received is untenable. As already discussed and at the sake of repetition, it is true that on the date of which the cause of action arose, the entire amount of the cheque was payable and any payment made subsequently, has already been acknowledged by the complainant side in post- notice evidence stage. Further defence in deposition of DW1 tried to bring in some business with Mohan Gold Water, however there is no such transaction or payment on record. The accused could have atleast proved the Directorship of Mohan Gold Water or proved some payments made to the said company to appropriate the payment towards the outstanding liability of complainant company. Accused also referred to some incentive on each carton and offer of one + one, however there is no proof to support any such contention. The invoices which shows supply of material i.e. beer to the accused records that there was 24% interest to be charged on any outstanding liability. Complainant company atleast proved some record, the accused however has merely tried to escape any liability by his oral testimony and there is no proof or atleast documentary proof attached to his testimony. FINAL CONCLUSION 41. It stands established on record in the form of evidence of the complainant given vide affidavit (which can be read in evidence at all stages as per judgment of " Rajesh Agarwal Vs. State & Anr. " 171 (2010) DELHI LAW TIMES 5), documents exhibited in evidence, admission(s) of accused during notice/accusations explained to him and statement Ct. Cases 17164 of 2017; P.S. Barakhamba Road Pages 22 of 23 Carlsberg Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchmukhi Enterprises of accused recorded under Section 313 of The Code of Criminal Procedure , 1973 read with Section 281 of The Code of Criminal Procedure , 1973 that complainant advanced financial assistance to the accused, accused issued cheques in question for discharge of liability, cheques got dishonored on presentment, complainant served legal demand notice upon accused demanding the cheques amount in question, however, accused failed to make the said payment within statutory period despite service. So, all the ingredients of offence punishable under Section 138 of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 stands established on record. The defence raised by accused side is not tenable/sustainable as per above discussions. The payment of Rs.6,00,000/- made by the accused to the complainant after the cause of action arose, is acknowledged by the complainant side to be qua the outstanding liability which was covered in the cheque amount. The same can be adjusted in the order on sentence. FINAL ORDER 42. In view of the aforementioned facts and circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that complainant has duly proved its case against the accused for offence punishable under Section 138 of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 beyond shadow of any reasonable doubt qua accused. Accordingly accused namely Mr. Ajay Tagi (proprietor of Panchmukhi Enterprises) stands convicted of the present cheque in question for offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
